name: BSD Zero Clause License
best_for: Small libraries, utilities, examples, and code where the author wants minimal friction.
watch_out: There is no express patent grant; review contributor and dependency patent risk separately.
compatibility: Generally easy to combine with permissive code because it adds no attribution condition.

name: MIT License
conditions: Preserve the copyright notice and permission notice
best_for: General-purpose applications, libraries, tools, and commercial-friendly open source.
watch_out: The short license is permissive, but it does not contain an express patent grant.
compatibility: Usually combines cleanly with other permissive code; preserve notices from every dependency.

name: MIT No Attribution License
best_for: Reusable code where downstream attribution should not be required.
watch_out: No express patent grant and no requirement to retain an attribution notice.
compatibility: Very permissive and generally easy to combine; still record its exact SPDX identifier.

name: BSD 2-Clause License
conditions: Preserve copyright, conditions, and disclaimer in source or documentation
best_for: Permissive libraries and infrastructure components with a concise attribution requirement.
watch_out: No express patent grant; notice placement still matters in binary distributions.
compatibility: Generally permissive; check any additional terms from dependencies before combining.

name: BSD 3-Clause License
conditions: Do not use the copyright holder name for endorsement without permission
best_for: Permissive software that wants an explicit non-endorsement clause.
watch_out: No express patent grant; avoid marketing language that implies endorsement.
compatibility: Generally permissive and broadly compatible, subject to notice and attribution requirements.

name: BSD 4-Clause License
best_for: Historical projects that already use the original BSD advertising-clause license.
watch_out: The advertising clause creates compatibility and compliance friction; avoid selecting it for new projects.
compatibility: More restrictive than BSD-2-Clause and BSD-3-Clause; not compatible with some copyleft licenses.

name: ISC License
conditions: Preserve the copyright and permission notice
best_for: Compact permissive libraries, especially in Unix and JavaScript ecosystems.
watch_out: No express patent grant; the short text should not be mistaken for a patent license.
compatibility: Usually easy to combine with MIT and BSD-style code.

name: Apache License 2.0
best_for: Commercial-friendly projects that want an express patent grant and clear contributor protections.
watch_out: Apache-2.0 is not automatically compatible with GPL-2.0-only; NOTICE and patent terms need deliberate handling.
compatibility: Generally compatible with GPL-3.0 and permissive licenses, but version-specific copyleft analysis is required.

name: zlib License
best_for: Small libraries and code intended to be embedded with minimal downstream obligations.
watch_out: The altered-source marking rule is easy to overlook; no express patent grant is stated.
compatibility: Generally permissive and compatible with most software licensing strategies.

name: PostgreSQL License
best_for: Permissive database and infrastructure software.
watch_out: Its permissive terms do not supply an express patent grant.
compatibility: Broadly permissive; keep the required notices in the appropriate distribution materials.

name: The Unlicense
best_for: Code intended to be as close as possible to public-domain dedication.
watch_out: Public-domain effectiveness varies by jurisdiction; the fallback license may be interpreted differently than a conventional license.
compatibility: Usually easy to combine, but some organizations prefer a conventional license for provenance and patent clarity.

name: Boost Software License 1.0
conditions: Preserve license notice in source distributions
best_for: C++ libraries and components following the Boost ecosystem’s permissive model.
watch_out: No express patent grant; check the specific component’s additional notices.
compatibility: Permissive and usually straightforward to combine with other open-source code.

name: Artistic License 2.0
conditions: Mark modified files or distinguish modified versions
best_for: Perl modules and projects that want the Artistic license family.
watch_out: Modified-version and standard-version provisions require more reading than MIT-style licenses.
compatibility: Generally permissive, but use the exact version and review the modified-work provisions.

name: Python License 2.0
best_for: Historical Python-related projects that already use this license.
watch_out: For a new project, compare it with a current, well-understood permissive license and avoid changing an existing project casually.
compatibility: Permissive in effect, but exact historical terms and notices should be retained.

name: PHP License 3.01
conditions: Do not use PHP trademarks or names for endorsement
best_for: Existing PHP ecosystem code that already carries this license.
watch_out: Name and endorsement restrictions are more specific than MIT; do not remove existing notices.
compatibility: Permissive but should be reviewed alongside downstream naming, attribution, and copyleft terms.

name: OpenSSL License
best_for: Historical OpenSSL/SSLeay-licensed code where the existing terms must be recognized.
watch_out: Do not confuse the legacy SPDX OpenSSL license with the Apache-2.0 licensing used by newer OpenSSL releases.
compatibility: Historical advertising or acknowledgement language can create compatibility friction; inspect the exact release.

name: libpng License
best_for: Existing PNG and image-processing code distributed under the libpng terms.
watch_out: Keep the original license notice and check whether a project includes additional third-party terms.
compatibility: Permissive in practice; treat the exact libpng notice as part of the distribution obligations.

name: University of Illinois/NCSA Open Source License
best_for: University-originated and historical permissive software.
watch_out: It has no express patent grant and may include acknowledgement language in the original notice.
compatibility: Usually compatible with permissive code; verify all notices before redistribution.

name: Academic Free License 3.0
best_for: Projects wanting permissive reuse with explicit copyright and patent grants.
watch_out: It is longer and more detailed than MIT; review its patent and notice provisions.
compatibility: Permissive, but its detailed language and patent provisions should be checked against copyleft terms.

name: Blue Oak Model License 1.0.0
conditions: Interpretation and patent language should be read in full
best_for: Projects that deliberately choose a modern, concise permissive license.
watch_out: It is less familiar to some compliance systems than MIT or Apache-2.0; test tooling support.
compatibility: Permissive in structure; verify organizational policy and SPDX tooling support before adoption.

name: Microsoft Public License
conditions: Distribute covered source modifications under the license
best_for: Existing Microsoft-originated components that already use the MS-PL.
watch_out: The reciprocal source condition and patent language need more review than a permissive license.
compatibility: Can combine with other code in some arrangements, but exact file boundaries and license compatibility matter.

name: Microsoft Reciprocal License
conditions: Make source of covered modifications available under the license
best_for: Existing Microsoft-originated code whose reciprocal terms are already established.
watch_out: It is more reciprocal than MS-PL; do not treat it as an MIT-style license.
compatibility: File-level structure can permit proprietary surrounding code, but compatibility must be checked case by case.

name: Mozilla Public License 2.0
conditions: Keep MPL-covered files under MPL-2.0 when distributed
Make modifications to covered files available
best_for: Libraries and applications that want open modifications at the file level while allowing larger combined works under other terms.
watch_out: Moving code between files can change the compliance analysis; track covered files and notices.
compatibility: Has a secondary-license mechanism for some combinations; do not assume compatibility without checking the exact terms.

name: Eclipse Public License 2.0
best_for: Enterprise and Java ecosystem projects that want a business-friendly reciprocal license.
watch_out: The definition of a modification and the secondary license option need careful application.
compatibility: EPL-2.0 has compatibility pathways, but exact license expressions and project structure still control the result.

name: Common Development and Distribution License 1.0
best_for: Existing Solaris, OpenSolaris, and related components already using CDDL.
watch_out: CDDL-1.0 has known incompatibility concerns with GPL-2.0-only; do not combine by intuition.
compatibility: File-level copyleft can coexist with proprietary files, but license compatibility analysis is essential.

name: GNU Lesser General Public License 2.1 only
conditions: Covered library modifications remain under LGPL-2.1
Provide source or relinkable object files as required
Allow reverse engineering for debugging changes
best_for: Libraries intended to be usable by proprietary applications under the LGPL-2.1 linking rules.
watch_out: Static linking, relinking, replacement libraries, and combined works require more than a simple notice.
compatibility: Can be relicensed to GPL-2.0 in the permitted cases, but LGPL-2.1-only is not the same as LGPL-2.1-or-later.

name: GNU Lesser General Public License 2.1 or later
conditions: Covered library modifications remain under a compatible LGPL version
Provide source or relinkable object files as required
Allow reverse engineering for debugging changes
best_for: Libraries that want LGPL-2.1 compatibility while allowing users to choose a later GNU version.
watch_out: The later-version option changes compatibility choices; record the exact expression in metadata.
compatibility: The or-later option offers more flexibility than LGPL-2.1-only; linking and source obligations remain.

name: GNU Lesser General Public License 3.0 only
conditions: Covered library modifications remain under LGPL-3.0
Provide source or relinkable object files as required
best_for: Libraries that want LGPL-3.0’s stronger patent and user-freedom provisions.
watch_out: The LGPL-3.0 family is based on GPL-3.0 and can impose more obligations than LGPL-2.1.
compatibility: Compatible combinations depend on the GPL/LGPL version and the linking model; review the full license.

name: GNU Lesser General Public License 3.0 or later
conditions: Covered library modifications remain under a compatible LGPL version
Provide source or relinkable object files as required
best_for: Libraries that want LGPL-3.0’s protections with the flexibility of a later-version option.
watch_out: Document whether your project uses LGPL-3.0-only or an or-later expression; they are not interchangeable.
compatibility: The later-version option can ease some compatibility decisions, but library linking obligations remain.

name: GNU General Public License 2.0 only
conditions: Distributed derivative or combined works generally remain under GPL-2.0
best_for: Projects that deliberately require the GPL-2.0 terms and ecosystem compatibility.
watch_out: GPL-2.0-only is not GPL-3.0 and is not automatically compatible with Apache-2.0 or every modern license.
compatibility: Permissive code is often usable under GPL-2.0, but the exact license and any advertising clause control compatibility.

name: GNU General Public License 2.0 or later
conditions: Distributed derivative or combined works generally remain under a compatible GPL version
best_for: GPL projects that want users to be able to choose GPL-2.0 or a later GPL version.
watch_out: The or-later permission can materially improve compatibility compared with GPL-2.0-only; state it precisely.
compatibility: Can often be used under GPL-3.0 when the combined work permits that choice; review all components and exceptions.

name: GNU General Public License 3.0 only
conditions: Distributed derivative or combined works generally remain under GPL-3.0
best_for: Projects requiring strong copyleft plus GPL-3.0 patent and user-device protections.
watch_out: GPL-3.0-only cannot simply be substituted for GPL-2.0-only in an existing dependency graph.
compatibility: Works with many permissive licenses, including Apache-2.0 in the relevant direction; exact expressions still matter.

name: GNU General Public License 3.0 or later
conditions: Distributed derivative or combined works generally remain under a compatible GPL version
best_for: New GPL projects that want GPL-3.0 protections and future-version flexibility.
watch_out: The later-version choice must be reflected consistently in source headers, documentation, and package metadata.
compatibility: Often the most flexible GPL-3 choice, but it does not remove the strong-copyleft and source obligations.

name: GNU Affero General Public License 3.0 only
conditions: Offer corresponding source to users interacting with a modified network service
best_for: Network services where the maintainers want modified server-side code to remain available to users.
watch_out: A hosted service can trigger obligations that ordinary GPL distribution would not; architecture and deployment model matter.
compatibility: AGPL-3.0 is closely related to GPL-3.0 but has additional network-use obligations; do not treat them as equivalent.

name: European Union Public License 1.2
conditions: Provide source for distributed derivative works
Copyleft with a defined compatibility list
best_for: European public-sector and international projects that want a multilingual, copyleft license with a compatibility list.
watch_out: The compatibility list and defined terms need to be read rather than inferred from GPL familiarity.
compatibility: EUPL-1.2 identifies compatible licenses in its terms; check the current license text and the direction of relicensing.

name: Open Software License 3.0
conditions: Provide source for distributed or externally deployed covered works
best_for: Projects that specifically want OSL’s external-deployment concept and strong reciprocal terms.
watch_out: External deployment language can matter for hosted offerings; it is not a simple GPL substitute.
compatibility: Strong copyleft and patent provisions require a focused compatibility review.

name: CeCILL 2.1
conditions: Provide source for distributed covered works
best_for: French and European research or public-sector software that uses the CeCILL family.
watch_out: Jurisdiction, governing-law, and compatibility provisions differ from GPL wording; read the complete text.
compatibility: Designed to be compatible with GPL-family licensing in specified ways, subject to the exact version and facts.

name: CeCILL-C
conditions: Covered library modifications remain under CeCILL-C
best_for: Libraries that want a CeCILL-compatible, weaker reciprocal model.
watch_out: The library boundary and French-law provisions should be reviewed with the same care as LGPL obligations.
compatibility: Library-oriented copyleft can allow broader combinations, but exact linking and compatibility facts control.

name: Q Public License 1.0
conditions: Covered library modifications remain under QPL
Restrictions on linking or distribution models may apply
best_for: Historical Qt and library code that already uses the QPL.
watch_out: The QPL is uncommon and has compatibility issues; do not select it for a new project without a specific reason.
compatibility: Review the exact linking and distribution provisions; it is not interchangeable with LGPL or MPL.

name: Sleepycat License
conditions: Covered derivative works must provide source under the license
best_for: Historical Berkeley DB components distributed under the Sleepycat terms.
watch_out: The source-availability trigger is important; many organizations instead choose a separately licensed commercial option.
compatibility: Library copyleft and historical terms require a specific review; do not assume compatibility with GPL or LGPL.

name: GNU Free Documentation License 1.3 only
conditions: Invariant sections or cover texts may apply
best_for: Manuals, textbooks, and documentation intentionally using GFDL’s copyleft model.
watch_out: GFDL is generally a poor choice for software source code and can create complex document-format obligations.
compatibility: Treat it as a documentation license; do not combine GFDL documentation terms with software code assumptions.

name: SIL Open Font License 1.1
conditions: Reserved Font Names may restrict modified font naming
Do not sell the font alone
best_for: Fonts and typeface files that need an open, embedding-friendly license.
watch_out: Do not use OFL as a general software license; font name, bundling, and standalone-sale provisions are specialized.
compatibility: Use for fonts; license the accompanying software, documentation, and artwork separately when necessary.

name: Creative Commons Zero 1.0 Universal
best_for: Datasets, metadata, media, and other non-software material intended for unrestricted reuse.
watch_out: Creative Commons does not recommend CC licenses for software; CC0 does not waive patent or trademark rights.
compatibility: Usually easy for content and data reuse; separate software and third-party rights still apply.

name: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International
best_for: Documentation, datasets, images, and other content where attribution is acceptable.
watch_out: Creative Commons recommends against using its licenses for software; confirm third-party content rights.
compatibility: Good for content reuse with attribution; do not treat it as an interchangeable software license.

name: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International
conditions: Share adaptations under the same or compatible terms
best_for: Documentation, educational content, and datasets where adaptations should remain shareable.
watch_out: ShareAlike is a content obligation, not a substitute for software copyleft analysis.
compatibility: Use for content and data; keep software code under a suitable software license.

name: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International
best_for: Non-commercial media or educational content where commercial reuse is intentionally restricted.
watch_out: NonCommercial is fact-sensitive and can block common business, advertising, training, or platform uses.
compatibility: Not an open-source software license; do not use it for code intended for broad commercial reuse.

name: Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International
best_for: Published content that may be redistributed unchanged but whose adapted versions should not be distributed.
watch_out: NoDerivatives conflicts with software modification and collaborative development; do not use it for source code.
compatibility: Content-focused and not an open-source software license.

name: Open Data Commons Attribution License 1.0
best_for: Open databases that need attribution without a database share-alike condition.
watch_out: Database rights, copyright, privacy, and contractual restrictions can exist independently of the license.
compatibility: Use for databases; the contents may carry separate terms and need their own review.

name: Open Data Commons Open Database License 1.0
conditions: Share adapted databases under ODbL or a compatible license
Provide or identify the source database
best_for: Collaborative databases where improvements to the database should remain open.
watch_out: ODbL distinguishes databases, contents, and produced works; the correct obligation depends on what you distribute.
compatibility: Database-specific share-alike rules should not be mapped directly onto software copyleft categories.

name: Business Source License 1.1
conditions: Use Limitation may restrict commercial use
Change Date may switch to a Change License
best_for: Products that intentionally use a time-delayed or use-limited source-available model.
watch_out: BUSL-1.1 is not an OSI-approved open-source license during the restricted period; its practical terms vary by project.
compatibility: Do not classify it as MIT-like or copyleft without reading the project-specific Additional Use Grant and Change License.
